subtopics.title: Key Facts & Formulas
subtopics.subtitle: One-page revision of the chapter's identities, counting rules and hardware constants

concepts.text: Digital logic and microprocessor questions are decided by a small set of identities, counting rules and hardware constants. This page collects them section by section; the wording matches the subtopics, so anything unclear here is explained there. Cover each block and rewrite it from memory before moving on.

concepts.latex: \text{Positional value: } N = \sum_i d_i\,b^i,\qquad n\text{ bits: } 0 \le N \le 2^n - 1
concepts.plainText: Positional value N = Σ d_i·b^i;  n unsigned bits cover 0 … 2^n − 1
Binary → Gray: MSB copied, then g_i = b_(i+1) XOR b_i
De Morgan: (AB)' = A' + B';  (A + B)' = A'·B'

concepts.latex: A + AB = A,\qquad A + \overline{A}B = A + B,\qquad AB + \overline{A}C + BC = AB + \overline{A}C
concepts.plainText: Absorption A + AB = A;  A + A'B = A + B;  consensus AB + A'C + BC = AB + A'C
XOR = AB' + A'B;  XNOR = AB + A'B'
A truth table has 2^n rows; there are 2^(2^n) Boolean functions of n variables
Minterm list ↔ maxterm list: F = Σm(S) = ΠM(complement set);  M_i = m_i'

concepts.latex: \text{K-map: } 2^k \text{ cells grouped} \Rightarrow n - k \text{ literals remain}
concepts.plainText: A K-map group of 2^k cells leaves n − k literals in the product term

concepts.latex: \text{MUX: } N \text{ inputs need } n = \log_2 N \text{ select lines}
concepts.plainText: An N:1 multiplexer needs log₂N select lines (4:1 → 2, 8:1 → 3, 16:1 → 4)
Decoder: n inputs → 2^n outputs;  encoder: 2^n inputs → n outputs

concepts.latex: \text{Half adder: } S = A \oplus B,\quad C = AB
concepts.plainText: Half adder: Sum = A XOR B, Carry = AB

concepts.latex: \text{Full adder: } S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{in},\quad C_{out} = AB + C_{in}(A \oplus B)
concepts.plainText: Full adder: Sum = A XOR B XOR C_in;  Carry = AB + C_in(A XOR B)
2's complement: invert and add 1;  n-bit range −2^(n−1) … 2^(n−1) − 1

concepts.latex: A - B = A + \overline{B} + 1,\qquad \text{overflow } V = C_n \oplus C_{n-1}
concepts.plainText: Subtract by adding the 2's complement;  overflow = carry-out XOR carry-into MSB

concepts.latex: Q^{+} = S + \overline{R}Q\ (SR),\qquad Q^{+} = J\overline{Q} + \overline{K}Q\ (JK),\qquad Q^{+} = T \oplus Q\ (T)
concepts.plainText: Characteristic equations: SR Q⁺ = S + R'Q;  JK Q⁺ = JQ' + K'Q;  T Q⁺ = T XOR Q;  D Q⁺ = D
Race-around in a level-triggered JK when the propagation delay is shorter than the clock pulse
n flip-flops: ring counter n states, Johnson (twisted-ring) 2n states
A MOD-N counter needs ⌈log₂N⌉ flip-flops and divides the clock by N
Ripple counter maximum clock = 1/(n·t_pd + t_decode)
n address lines address 2^n locations: 8085 16 lines → 64 KB, 8086 20 lines → 1 MB
8086 physical address = segment × 16 + offset;  each segment is 64 KB
8086 effective address = base + index + displacement (BX/BP + SI/DI + disp)
8085: RST n vectors to 8n;  TRAP 0024H, RST 5.5 002CH, RST 6.5 0034H, RST 7.5 003CH
One T-state = 1/f_clk;  PUSH decrements SP by 2, POP increments by 2

concepts.latex: \text{MUL: } AX = AL \times r8,\ DX{:}AX = AX \times r16;\quad \text{DIV: } AL = AX \div r8,\ AH = \text{remainder}
concepts.plainText: MUL r8 → AX; MUL r16 → DX:AX;  DIV r8 → quotient AL, remainder AH
Chips needed = total memory ÷ chip size;  8085 isolated I/O has 256 ports
8255 PPI: ports A, B, C = 24 lines; modes 0 (basic), 1 (strobed), 2 (bidirectional), BSR
Bit time = 1/bit rate;  characters per second = baud ÷ frame bits (8N1 = 10 bits)
Bit rate = baud × log₂(levels per symbol)

concepts.latex: \text{DMA burst time } T = N \times t_{cycle};\qquad \text{8237: 4 channels, 64 KB blocks}
concepts.plainText: Burst DMA: N transfers × cycle time;  8237 has 4 channels and 64 KB maximum block

concepts.latex: \text{8086 vector address} = 4n;\quad IP \leftarrow M[4n],\ CS \leftarrow M[4n+2]
concepts.plainText: 8086 INT n vector at address 4n: IP from 4n, CS from 4n + 2
Interrupt vector table: 256 entries × 4 bytes = 1 KB at 00000H–003FFH

concepts.latex: \text{Interrupt pushes FLAGS, CS, IP: } SP \leftarrow SP - 6;\qquad \text{8259: } 8 \times 8 = 64 \text{ lines}
concepts.plainText: An 8086 interrupt pushes FLAGS, CS and IP (SP − 6);  one master + 8 slave 8259s give 64 lines

rows: 8 bit / 16 bit, 64 KB, 3 MHz (6 MHz crystal ÷ 2)
8086: data / address bus, memory, prefetch queue
9 = 6 status (CF PF AF ZF SF OF) + 3 control (TF IF DF)
Ripple: n·t_pd accumulates;  synchronous: one flip-flop delay

concepts.text: The sheet above lists the rules; this drill applies each one once as a short worked calculation. Work every line yourself with the answer covered, then compare. Each line is a single step or two, so the aim is speed with the radix, the direction of the shift and the off-by-one kept right.

concepts.plainText: Sign-magnitude and 1's complement: −(2^(n−1) − 1) to 2^(n−1) − 1;  2's complement: −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1

concepts.text:
K-maps and counters
3-variable map: 8 cells ; a quad leaves 3 - 2 = 1 literal
4-variable map: 16 cells ; pair -> 3 literals, octet -> 1 literal
MOD-6:  4 < 6 <= 8        -> 3 flip-flops, 8 - 6 = 2 unused states
MOD-10 ripple: 4 flip-flops, clear at 1010 -> NAND(Q3, Q1)
4 flip-flops: ring MOD-4, Johnson MOD-8, binary MOD-16
1 MHz into a 5-bit Johnson (MOD-10) -> 100 kHz

Addresses and memory
8 KB block from 2000H: end = 2000H + 1FFFH      = 3FFFH
32 KB from 8K x 8 chips: 32K/8K = 4 chips
   A0-A12 (13 lines) to every chip, A13-A14 -> 2-to-4 decoder
16K x 8 from 4K x 4: (16K x 8)/(4K x 4) = 8 chips (4 rows of 2)
1234H:0056H -> 12340H + 0056H                   = 12396H
[BP+DI+10H], BP = 0200H, DI = 0030H -> EA = 0240H in SS

concepts.plainText: End address = start + size − 1;  chips = (M words × W bits) ÷ (m words × w bits per chip)

concepts.text:
Serial timing, DMA and vectors
4800 baud, 8N1 (1+8+1 = 10 bits) -> 480 char/s, bit time 208.3 us
9600 baud, 7E1 (1+7+1+1 = 10 bits) -> 960 char/s
8251 at 9600 baud with x64 factor -> TxC = 614.4 kHz
Burst DMA of 1 KB at 0.5 us per transfer -> 1024 x 0.5 = 512 us
INT 21H: 4 x 21H = 84H -> IP at 00084H, CS at 00086H
RST 7 -> 7 x 8 = 38H ; RST 5.5 -> 5.5 x 8 = 44 = 002CH

rows: Synchronous and asynchronous; baud factor x1, x16, x64
4 channels, up to 64 KB per block
4 channels, 14-bit count, up to 16 KB per block
8 IR inputs; 64 with one master and 8 slaves

concepts.text: The usual slips in this chapter are off-by-one errors: an address range ends at start + size − 1, a counter needing N states is not always full so unused states remain, and a 2's complement range has one more negative value than positive. Keep hex arithmetic in hex; 1FFFH + 1 is 2000H, not 2000 decimal.
For any numeric question, first write the one-line rule, then substitute. Speed comes from recognising the rule (2^n, log₂N, 4n, 8n, × 10H, baud ÷ frame bits), not from calculating faster.

formulas.latex: S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{in},\qquad C_{out} = AB + C_{in}(A \oplus B)

formulas.plainText: Flip-flops for MOD-N and its frequency division

notes.text: Counting rules answer half the numeric MCQs: 2^n rows, 2^n locations, log₂N select lines, ⌈log₂N⌉ flip-flops, 4n and 8n vector addresses. Decide which rule a question is hiding before reaching for a calculator.

Hexadecimal traps: segment × 10H means shift left by one hex digit, not multiply by ten; a 20-bit physical address has five hex digits; INT 21H is type 33 decimal, so its vector is at 4 × 33 = 132 = 00084H.

Pairs that get swapped: NAND/NOR are universal (AND/OR are not); ring counter n states, Johnson 2n; TRAP is non-maskable in the 8085, NMI in the 8086; PUSH decrements SP, POP increments it; MUL widens (AL × r8 → AX), DIV narrows (AX ÷ r8 → AL, AH).

formulas.title: De Morgan's theorems
formulas.description: Break the bar, change the operator; applies to any number of variables.

formulas.title: Full adder
formulas.latex: S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{in},\qquad C_{out} = AB + C_{in}(A \oplus B)
formulas.plainText: Sum = A XOR B XOR C_in;  Carry = AB + C_in(A XOR B)
formulas.description: Three inputs, two outputs; the carry is the majority function.

formulas.title: MOD-N counter
formulas.plainText: Flip-flops n = ceil(log₂N);  f_out = f_in / N
formulas.description: N is the modulus (number of states); f_in the clock frequency.

formulas.title: 8086 physical address
formulas.description: 20-bit result; the segment is shifted left one hex digit before adding the 16-bit offset.

formulas.title: Interrupt vectors
formulas.plainText: 8086 INT n vector at 4n;  8085 RST n vector at 8n
formulas.description: n is the interrupt type (8086) or the RST number 0–7 (8085).

flashcards.front: State both De Morgan theorems and the XOR expansion.
Give the 8086 physical-address formula and the 8086/8085 interrupt vector rules.
flashcards.back: PA = segment × 10H + offset; 8086 INT n → address 4n (IP at 4n, CS at 4n + 2); 8085 RST n → 8n.

flashcards.front: How many flip-flops for a MOD-12 counter, and what output frequency from a 12 kHz clock?

questions.questionText: A synchronous counter is required to divide a 6 MHz clock by 24. The minimum number of flip-flops and the output frequency are:
questions.explanation: 2^4 = 16 < 24 ≤ 32 = 2^5, so 5 flip-flops are needed; f_out = 6 MHz / 24 = 250 kHz.

questions.questionText: In an 8086 system, the interrupt vector for INT 10H is stored starting at physical address:
questions.explanation: Vector address = 4 × type = 4 × 10H = 40H, i.e. 00040H; IP is read from 00040H and CS from 00042H.

questions.questionText: The 8-bit 2's complement representation of −40 is:
With SS = 3000H and SP = 0100H, the physical address of the top of the 8086 stack is:
The Boolean expression (A + B)(A + C) simplifies to:
questions.explanation: By the distributive law of OR over AND, (A + B)(A + C) = A + BC; expanding gives A + AC + AB + BC = A + BC after absorption.

questions.questionText: The value of 1011₂ + 27₈ + 1AH, written in decimal, is:
questions.explanation: Convert each term: 1011₂ = 11, 27₈ = 2 × 8 + 7 = 23, 1AH = 16 + 10 = 26; 11 + 23 + 26 = 60. Reading 27₈ as decimal 27 gives the wrong total 64.

questions.questionText: Which of the following numbers has the largest value?
The hexadecimal subtraction 5A3H − 2C7H gives:
questions.explanation: Units: 3 − 7 needs a borrow, 19 − 7 = 12 = C; sixteens: (A − 1) − C = 9 − 12 needs a borrow, 25 − 12 = 13 = D; 256s: (5 − 1) − 2 = 2. Result 2DCH (check: 1443 − 711 = 732 = 2DCH). 3DCH forgets the last borrow.

questions.questionText: The binary product 1011₂ × 1101₂ is:
Which decimal fraction can be represented EXACTLY with a finite number of binary digits?
questions.explanation: 0.375 = 3/8 = 0.011₂, a denominator that is a power of 2. 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 have a factor 5 in their denominators, so their binary expansions repeat forever (0.1 = 0.000110011…₂).

questions.questionText: One byte is used to hold a number. The largest value it can hold as unsigned binary and as packed BCD (two digits) is:
questions.explanation: Unsigned binary: 1111 1111 = 2⁸ − 1 = 255. Packed BCD stores two decimal digits of 4 bits each, and the largest is 1001 1001 = 99, since codes above 1001 are invalid.

questions.questionText: The packed BCD byte 1001 0110 (96H) is converted to a pure binary number. The binary result, in hexadecimal, is:
questions.explanation: The BCD digits mean 9 and 6, i.e. 96 decimal = 64 + 32 = 0110 0000₂ = 60H. 0906H is the unpacked BCD form and 5AH = 90 drops the units digit.

questions.questionText: The 8-bit 2's complement number F6H is sign-extended to 16 bits and then added to 0020H in a 16-bit adder (carry out ignored). The 16-bit result is:
questions.explanation: Sign extension copies bit 7 into the high byte: F6H → FFF6H (−10). FFF6H + 0020H = 1 0016H, and dropping the carry leaves 0016H = +22 = −10 + 32. 0116H results from zero-extending instead (246 + 32).

questions.questionText: An 8-bit ALU adds 6BH and 2DH. Which statement about the result is correct?
options: The result is 98H: correct both as unsigned and as signed
The result is 98H: correct as unsigned (152), but a signed overflow (V = 1)
The result is 98H with a carry out, so the unsigned result is wrong
The result is 88H with no overflow
questions.explanation: 6BH + 2DH = 107 + 45 = 152 = 98H, which fits in 8 unsigned bits (C = 0). As signed numbers, two positives gave a result with bit 7 = 1 (−104), so V = 1.

questions.questionText: An 8-bit ALU adds F0H and 10H. Which statement about the result is correct?
options: The 8-bit result is 00H with C = 0 and V = 1: correct as unsigned, wrong as signed
The 8-bit result is 00H with carry C = 1 and V = 0: wrong as unsigned, correct as signed
The 8-bit result is 00H with C = 1 and V = 1: wrong both as unsigned and as signed
The 8-bit result is 100H with no carry
questions.explanation: Unsigned 240 + 16 = 256 does not fit in 8 bits, so C = 1 and the byte 00H is wrong as unsigned. Signed −16 + 16 = 0 is correct; the carries into and out of bit 7 are both 1, so V = 0.

questions.questionText: A 2-input NOR gate is fed by A and B, and its output drives one input of a 2-input NAND gate whose other input is C. The NAND output is:
questions.explanation: The NOR gives (A + B)'. The NAND gives [(A + B)'·C]' = (A + B)'' + C' = A + B + C' by De Morgan's theorem.

questions.questionText: The expression (A + B')(A' + B) simplifies to:
questions.explanation: Expanding: AA' + AB + A'B' + BB' = 0 + AB + A'B' + 0 = AB + A'B', which is A XNOR B (1 when A = B).

questions.questionText: The function F = A'B + AC written in minimal product-of-sums form is:
questions.explanation: Check: (A + B)(A' + C) = AA' + AC + A'B + BC = AC + A'B + BC, and BC is the consensus of AC and A'B, so it equals A'B + AC. When A = 0 the POS reduces to B and when A = 1 to C, matching the SOP.

questions.questionText: When an 8085 program is translated to 8086 code using Intel's standard register correspondence, the 8085 HL pair (the memory pointer M) maps to:
questions.explanation: The standard mapping is A → AL, BC → CX, DE → DX and HL → BX (H → BH, L → BL). BX is the 8086 general register that can serve as a memory pointer, just as HL does in MOV A, M.

questions.questionText: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(2, 3, 10) + d(6, 7, 11), where d marks don't-cares. The minimal SOP form of F is:
questions.explanation: Taking don't-care 11 as 1, cells 2, 3, 10, 11 (B = 0, C = 1) form a quad, giving B'C; cells 6 and 7 are left as 0. A'C misses minterm 10, B'CD' misses minterm 3, and A'B'C + AB'CD' is correct but not minimal.

questions.questionText: Using a K-map, F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 1, 2, 3, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15) simplifies to:
questions.explanation: Minterms 0–3 and 8–11 (all with B = 0) form an octet giving B'. Minterms 10, 11, 14, 15 (A = 1, C = 1) form a quad giving AC, so F = B' + AC.

questions.questionText: F(A, B, C, D) = 1 when the unsigned number ABCD (A = MSB) is a multiple of 3, including 0. How many product terms does its minimal SOP form contain?
questions.explanation: The minterms are 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 (0000, 0011, 0110, 1001, 1100, 1111). Every pair differs in at least two bits, so no two are adjacent on the K-map; each minterm is its own prime implicant, giving 6 four-literal terms.

questions.questionText: The eight outputs Y0–Y7 of an enabled 3-to-8 decoder (active-high) are connected to inputs D0–D7 of an 8-to-3 encoder in the same order. If the decoder input is 101, the encoder output is:
options: 010, the bitwise complement of the input
101, the same as the decoder input
Undefined, because several encoder inputs are active
questions.explanation: Input 101 makes only Y5 HIGH, so only D5 of the encoder is active and it outputs 5 = 101. A decoder followed by the matching encoder simply passes the code through; only one line is ever active, so no priority is needed.

questions.questionText: The 8085 instruction STA 2050H (opcode 32H) is stored starting at address 3000H. The bytes at 3000H, 3001H and 3002H are:
questions.explanation: The opcode comes first, followed by the 16-bit address with its low byte first (little-endian): 32H at 3000H, 50H at 3001H and 20H at 3002H.

questions.questionText: A 16-bit ripple-carry adder with no carry input is to be built with the fewest gates, using full adders and half adders. It needs:
questions.explanation: The least significant bit has only two inputs, so a half adder suffices there; each of the other 15 bits must also add the incoming carry and needs a full adder.

questions.questionText: A JK flip-flop has its J input connected to its own Q' output and its K input connected to its own Q output. On every active clock edge it:
questions.explanation: Q⁺ = JQ' + K'Q = Q'·Q' + Q'·Q = Q'. When Q = 0 the inputs are J = 1, K = 0 (set); when Q = 1 they are J = 0, K = 1 (reset), so the output toggles like a T flip-flop with T = 1.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit synchronous counter uses T flip-flops with T0 = 1, T1 = Q0, T2 = Q0·Q1 and T3 = Q0·Q1·Q2. In state Q3 Q2 Q1 Q0 = 1011, the next state is:
questions.explanation: With Q0 = Q1 = 1 and Q2 = 0: T0 = 1, T1 = 1, T2 = 1, T3 = 0. Q0, Q1, Q2 toggle and Q3 holds, giving 1100 (11 + 1 = 12), as expected for a binary up counter.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit binary up counter is loaded with 1011 and then receives 9 clock pulses. Its final state is:
questions.explanation: The count goes 11 → 11 + 9 = 20, and a 4-bit counter wraps at 16, so the state is 20 − 16 = 4 = 0100. 0011 is one pulse short.

questions.questionText: A 3-bit synchronous binary counter clocked at 8 MHz drives a 3-to-8 decoder with active-high outputs. The waveform at output Y5 has a frequency and duty cycle of:
questions.explanation: The counter has 8 states, so each decoder output goes HIGH once every 8 clocks: f = 8 MHz ÷ 8 = 1 MHz. It stays HIGH for 1 clock of the 8, so the duty cycle is 1/8 = 12.5%.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, MVI A, 0C5H; ANI 3CH; XRI 0FFH are executed. The accumulator then holds:
questions.explanation: C5H AND 3CH = 1100 0101 AND 0011 1100 = 0000 0100 = 04H; XOR with FFH inverts every bit: 1111 1011 = FBH. 02H would come from ORI 3CH instead of ANI 3CH.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, MVI A, 20H; SUI 30H; CMA; INR A are executed. The final accumulator and CY flag are:
questions.explanation: SUI: 20H − 30H = F0H with a borrow, so CY = 1. CMA gives 0FH and INR A gives 10H, i.e. the 2's complement of F0H, the magnitude of the negative result. Neither CMA nor INR changes CY, so it stays 1.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, DE = 0035H. The program MOV A, E; CMA; MOV E, A; MOV A, D; CMA; MOV D, A; INX D is executed. DE now holds:
questions.explanation: Complementing both bytes gives FFCAH (the 1's complement) and INX D adds 1, giving FFCBH, the 16-bit 2's complement of 0035H (−53). 8035H is the sign-magnitude form.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, MVI A, 64H is followed by two RRC instructions. The accumulator and CY are then:
questions.explanation: 64H = 0110 0100. RRC → 0011 0010 (32H), CY = 0; RRC → 0001 1001 (19H), CY = 0. Because the two bits rotated out were 0, this equals dividing 100 by 4 = 25 = 19H. 91H is the result of two RLCs.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, the packed BCD byte 47H is split by MVI A, 47H; ANI 0F0H; RRC; RRC; RRC; RRC. The accumulator finally holds:
questions.explanation: ANI 0F0H keeps the high digit: 40H. Four RRCs rotate the byte right by four places, moving the high nibble into the low nibble: 0100 0000 → 0000 0100 = 04H, the unpacked tens digit.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, LXI H, 20FFH; INR L; MOV M, A are executed. MOV M, A writes the accumulator to address:
questions.explanation: INR L is an 8-bit increment: L goes from FFH to 00H (setting Z) and no carry passes into H, so HL = 2000H. INX H would have given 2100H.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, SP = 2400H, BC = 5678H and DE = 1234H. After PUSH B, PUSH D and then POP H, the contents of HL and SP are:
questions.explanation: Each PUSH lowers SP by 2: PUSH B → 23FEH, PUSH D → 23FCH. POP H takes the last pair pushed (DE = 1234H; L from 23FCH, H from 23FDH) and raises SP by 2 to 23FEH.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AL = 05H. After NEG AL, AL and CF are:
questions.explanation: NEG forms the 2's complement (0 − AL): 00H − 05H = FBH (−5), and CF = 1 because the operand was not zero. FAH is only the 1's complement and 85H the sign-magnitude form.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, CMP AX, AX is executed (AX holds any value). Which result is correct?
options: ZF = 1, CF = 0, SF = 0, PF = 0; AX unchanged
ZF = 1, CF = 0, SF = 0, PF = 1; AX unchanged
questions.explanation: CMP subtracts without storing the result, so AX is unchanged. AX − AX = 0 gives ZF = 1, no borrow (CF = 0), sign bit 0 (SF = 0), and the low byte 00H has an even number (zero) of 1s, so PF = 1.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AX = 1234H and CL = 04H. After ROL AX, CL, AX and CF are:
questions.explanation: Rotating left by 4 moves the top hex digit to the bottom: 1234H → 2341H. After ROL, CF holds the last bit rotated out of the MSB, which is now bit 0 of the result (1). 4123H would be ROR and 2340H would be SHL.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AX = 7FFFH and CF = 1. After INC AX, which result is correct?
questions.explanation: 7FFFH + 1 = 8000H: +32767 + 1 cannot be represented in 16 signed bits, so OF = 1, and bit 15 is 1, so SF = 1. INC does not affect CF, which keeps its old value 1.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AL = F0H and BL = 10H. After MUL BL, the contents of AX and the CF/OF flags are:
questions.explanation: MUL BL computes AX = AL × BL = F0H × 10H = 240 × 16 = 3840 = 0F00H. Because the upper half AH = 0FH is not zero, CF and OF are both set to 1.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AX = FFF9H and BL = 02H. After IDIV BL (signed division), AL and AH contain:
questions.explanation: AX = FFF9H = −7 and BL = +2. IDIV rounds the quotient toward zero, so −7 ÷ 2 = −3 (FDH) in AL, and the remainder takes the sign of the dividend: −7 − (−3 × 2) = −1 (FFH) in AH.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, CX = 0000H when a loop body ending in LOOP L is entered from the top. How many times does the body execute?
questions.explanation: LOOP first decrements CX and then jumps if CX ≠ 0. The first decrement turns 0000H into FFFFH, so the loop continues until CX has counted all the way down: 65536 passes in total. JCXZ is used before such loops to skip them when CX = 0.

questions.questionText: An 8086 runs at 5 MHz, and each bus cycle takes 4 clock periods and fetches one aligned word. With no wait states, and with the EU taking no bytes from the queue meanwhile, how long does the BIU need to fill its empty 6-byte instruction queue?
questions.explanation: 6 bytes ÷ 2 bytes per bus cycle = 3 bus cycles; each bus cycle = 4 × 200 ns = 800 ns, so 3 × 0.8 µs = 2.4 µs. 4.8 µs assumes one byte per bus cycle.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, DS = 7A00H. The data segment covers the physical addresses:
questions.explanation: Base = 7A00H × 10H = 7A000H; a segment spans 64 KB, so the last address is 7A000H + FFFFH = 89FFFH. 8A000H is one past the end.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the 8086 instruction LAHF is correct?
options: It copies SF, ZF, AF, PF and CF (the low byte of FLAGS, laid out like the 8085 flag register) into AH
It copies all 16 bits of FLAGS into AX
It loads AH from the memory byte addressed by the flags
It copies OF, DF, IF and TF into AH
questions.explanation: LAHF (load AH from flags) moves the low byte of FLAGS, which holds SF, ZF, AF, PF and CF in the same bit positions as the 8085 flag register, into AH. SAHF does the reverse; the high-byte flags OF, DF, IF and TF are not included.

questions.questionText: Compared with the 8085, the 8086 has how many more address lines, and how many times larger is its directly addressable memory?
questions.explanation: The 8085 has 16 address lines (2¹⁶ = 64 KB) and the 8086 has 20 (2²⁰ = 1 MB). Each extra line doubles the space, so 4 extra lines give 2⁴ = 16 times more memory.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is NOT correct?
options: The 8086 has a 6-byte instruction prefetch queue
The 8085 multiplexes its lower address byte with data on AD0–AD7
The 8086 can address 1 MB of memory with its 20 address lines
questions.explanation: The 8085 has an 8-bit data bus and a 16-bit address bus; the other three statements are correct.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly compares interrupt vectors in the 8085 and the 8086?
options: 8085 RST vectors are fixed code addresses 8 bytes apart; each 8086 vector is a 4-byte CS:IP pointer in a 1 KB table
Both processors use a 256-entry pointer table at address 00000H
Each 8086 vector is a fixed code address 8 bytes apart, as in the 8085
8085 vectors are 4-byte pointers and 8086 vectors are 8-byte code areas
questions.explanation: An 8085 RST n jumps directly to code at 8n (0000H, 0008H, … 0038H). The 8086 reads a 4-byte pointer (IP then CS) from address 4n; 256 × 4 bytes = 1 KB at 00000H–003FFH.

questions.questionText: Which of the following does NOT cause an interrupt in the 8086?
options: Executing DIV with a zero divisor
questions.explanation: HLT only stops the processor until an interrupt or reset arrives. A zero divisor causes type 0, INTO with OF = 1 causes type 4, and TF = 1 causes the single-step type 1 interrupt.
